📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Is Bitcoin’s worst Q4 on record getting closer?

The last 24 hours may have served as a reality check for investors. Bitcoin broke below the $62,000-level for the first time since August. However, the sharp decline may not be an isolated move. The sell-off followed the release of the latest FOMC minutes, adding to concerns over the Fed’s next policy move.

So, with Q4 already shaping up to be one of Bitcoin’s weakest quarters, could the worst be yet to come?

The latest FOMC minutes could be an early warning sign for Bitcoin’s Q4 outlook.

According to the minutes, almost all Fed officials now expect more rate hikes to bring inflation back to the 2% target. Some even suggested that a 50-basis-point hike could be on the table if inflation data worsens. In this context, Bitcoin’s latest correction suggests that investors may be taking a bearish view of the report. It is set to lay the tone for the next Fed meeting, scheduled for 10th December.

In short, the Fed maintained interest rates at 3.75%-4% in October, but the minutes have now strengthened expectations of another December hike. Here, it’s worth pointing out that market expectations already reflect this shift.

According to CME data, for instance, the odds of a rate hike have reached 100%. Of this, 92.7% of traders expect a 25-basis-point hike, taking rates to 4%-4.25%. The remaining 7.3% expect a bigger, 50-basis-point hike to 4.25%-4.5%.

Meanwhile, the pressure is also showing up in traditional markets.

In a recent development, the Dollar Index rose to 103.82 on 18th November, its highest level since April 2025. As a result, yields on U.S 10-year Treasuries rose above 5.1%. Also, it seems increasingly likely that if this continues, traditional assets will become more appealing than riskier assets. This is likely due to the hawkish tone of the FOMC minutes which said,.

Almost all participants judged that further action to raise the target range for the federal funds rate would likely be appropriate.

Bitcoin’s [BTC] Q4 decline is getting closer to its 2018 record now.

As the chart below highlights, Bitcoin is down 24.45% in Q4 2026, with November’s 18.48% decline accelerating the correction. This puts BTC on track for one of its weakest fourth quarters on record. The closest historical comparison is Q4 2018, when Bitcoin fell by 43.5% during the bear market.

Sure, the prevailing decline is still 19.05% short of that record. However, this is where the latest FOMC minutes come into play. The release has added to concerns across the crypto market, with traders now weighing the possibility of further rate hikes.

If these expectations continue to rise, Bitcoin could face more selling pressure, pushing its Q4 decline closer to the 2018 record.

However, the bigger question is whether this selling pressure can continue or not.

According to recent reports, with rate hikes now almost fully priced in, the focus will shift to whether Bitcoin has enough demand to absorb further selling. This would make on-chain activity and institutional flows key indicators to watch. At the time of writing though, the signals were not encouraging.

In fact, according to a recent Wintermute report,.

With flows negative and the 200-week lost, December Fed hike is priced at about 92% after core CPI printed 0.3% for a third month, and spot Bitcoin ETFs are $1.9B net negative for 2026. We expect pressure into the $50s, with Saturday’s $62K low the first level and the $60K put cluster on Deribit the next magnet.

To understand how the macro environment could affect Bitcoin’s Q4 performance, the focus should also be on key on-chain data.

According to Glassnode’s latest report, Bitcoin has been facing strong selling pressure. Investors are booking losses at levels last seen near major market bottoms in 2018, 2020 and 2022. However, the $62K-66K range is acting as a key support zone, with nearly 20% of short-term holder supply sitting in this range.

That’s not all though. According to CryptoQuant, Bitcoin’s 30-day Net Realized Profit/Loss dropped to -$8.4 billion recently, its lowest level since the summer. Selling has accelerated too, with investors realizing $5.4 billion in losses between 15th-18th November alone. Even long-term holders have been selling at a loss, with their SOPR falling to 0.73 — its lowest level since August.

Sources indicate that the key takeaway? The ongoing losses are still lower than those seen during the February (30 billion) and June (18.4 billion) bottoms. This means that Bitcoin may not have reached full capitulation “yet.”.

So, if Bitcoin falls below $60K, this could lead to liquidations of nearly 20% of the short-term supply.

Considering the hawkish Fed, bearish technicals, and negative on-chain signals, a further downtrend cannot be ruled out. In fact, Wintermute now anticipates a further decline, with $50K now becoming a possible downside target for BTC.

The comparison with gold adds another layer to the picture.

Sources indicate that from a technical perspective, Bitcoin has been flashing signs of some positive momentum relative to gold. On 18th November, the Bitcoin-to-Gold rate rose above its 200-day simple moving average to 17.13 ounces of gold for one Bitcoin. However, the broader trend might tell us a different story.

Despite this recovery, however, the BTC/XAU ratio was still down nearly 16% in Q4 at press time.

According to recent reports, in other words, while Bitcoin has bounced against gold in the short term, it continues to underperform over the quarter. So, for long-term holders, gold still has the upper hand, while Bitcoin needs a stronger recovery to close the performance gap.

This finding also brings the cautious FOMC minutes back into focus.

Bitcoin now needs stronger spot demand, ETF inflows and a recovery in the BTC/XAU ratio to limit further losses. However, ongoing capitulation raises concerns about whether buyers can absorb the pressure. With the next FOMC meeting adding to market uncertainty, Wintermute’s $50K downside target will be in play.

Sources indicate that technically, that would pull Bitcoin nearly 40% lower in Q4. If selling pressure continues, the possibility of Bitcoin’s Q4 correction surpassing 2018’s record cannot be ruled out.

Bitcoin’s Q4 decline hit 24.45%, with weak on-chain data, ETF outflows, and hawkish Fed expectations adding to selling pressure.

A drop to $50K could push Bitcoin’s Q4 losses close to 40%, putting 2018’s record within reach.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • BYD opened pre-orders for the third-generation Tang starting at about $34,000 in China.
  • The third-generation Tang joins the Great Tang, or Da Tang, as it’s called in China in BYD’s expanding flagship SUV lineup.
  • We knew it was coming soon after the newly introduced model appeared in a regulatory filing in China’s Ministry of Industry and Information Technology (MIIT) last month.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

BYD opened pre-orders for the third-generation Tang starting at about $34,000 in China. This five-seat flagship SUV packs more than you’d expect for the money, with two massive 30-inch-plus screens inside and up to 850 km (528 miles) of CLTC range.

The third-generation Tang joins the Great Tang, or Da Tang, as it’s called in China in BYD’s expanding flagship SUV lineup.

We knew it was coming soon after the newly introduced model appeared in a regulatory filing in China’s Ministry of Industry and Information Technology (MIIT) last month.

BYD confirmed on Friday that pre-orders for the third-gen Tang are officially open, starting at 225,000 yuan, which is around $34,000.

The “large five-seat flagship SUV,” as BYD calls it, is available in three variants, priced from 225,000 yuan ($34,000), 240,000 yuan ($36,000), and 260,000 yuan ($39,000) with rear- and all-wheel-drive variants.

The two lower-priced variants are both RWD, offering a CLTC range of up to 850 km (528 miles), while the top-spec dual-motor AWD version has up to 770 km (478 miles).

All versions use BYD’s second-generation Blade Batteries and Flash Charging tech, enabling the battery to be charged from 10% to 80% in five minutes, or nine minutes to go from 10% to 97%.

Industry observers note that inside, the five-seat SUV packs a surprising amount of tech and premium extras for the price. The setup features two massive screens: a 35.4″ integrated display and another 30″ panoramic theater screen.

Unlike its predessor, which offered five and six-seat configurations, the third-gen Tang will only be offered as a five-seater.

The five-seat setup opens up interior space for passengers and the third-gen Tang has the largest front trunk (frunk) in its class at 205L, BYD noted.

Like many of its new flagship vehicles, the third-gen Tang is equipped with BYD’s latest tech, including its God’s Eye B driver-assistance system and Disus-A dual-chamber intelligent air suspension body control system.

Other added features include a 22-speaker Dynaudio sound system, intelligent electric all‑wheel drive, a high-speed tire blowout stability system, and its iTAC intelligent torque control system.

Lu Tian, the general manager of BYD’s Dynasty division noted third-gen Tang vehicles have arrived at dealerships nationwide.

Why mention "two enormous screens" like they are some markers of a more premium vehicle or represent some value? We don't measure the utility of cars by screen real estate per dollar. It's the other part of the utility that matter: range, driving dynamics, road trip convenience, fit/finish/materials/insulation. Personally, I don't think "enormous screens" are going to age well as an automotive trend.

The Great Tang received over 150,000 preorders by the time it launched in mid-June, a record for a single BYD model.

Since its official launch, the larger Great Tang (Da Tang) has sold more than 10,000 units for four straight months now.

The Great Tang is on sale in China in pure electric (EV) and plug-in hybrid (PHEV) powertrains. The cheapest EV variant starts at 239,900 yuan ($35,500) a CLTC driving range of 800 km (497 miles). Starting at just 269,900 yuan ($40,000), the Flagship EV version uses a bigger (130.15 kWh) battery, offering a CLTC range of up to 590 miles (950 km).

Will BYD’s smaller five-seat SUV draw the same demand? Let us know your thoughts in the comments below.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Cryptocurrency prices are bouncing back, with Bitcoin (BTC), XRP and Shiba Inu (SHIB) all in the green after the surprising announcement that Jensen Huang has been reappointed as chief executive officer of Nvidia.

The sudden leadership reversal comes as tech stocks bounce back following the sharp market sell-off that has also affected major crypto assets.

Recent findings suggest that nvidia made a major announcement on Monday, Nov. 23, stating that its board of directors had unanimously approved Huang's reappointment as the manufacturer’s president, CEO, and a board director, effective immediately.

The news is a surprise move by the tech giant, which had previously remarked that Huang, the tech giant’s longtime CEO, wouldn’t be coming back after his resignation earlier this month.

As stated in Nvidia’s official press release, the board made its decision following a series of discussions with Huang.

Additionally, the manufacturer consulted with high-ranking U.S. government officials to determine that the reappointment would not present a national security concern.

Huang himself acknowledged the reappointment, thanking employees, shareholders and the firm’s leaders.

“I can’t wait to get back to work,” noted Huang.

The firm also mentioned that the independent inquiry into the events leading to Huang’s departure would continue.

According to recent reports, the news of Huang’s reappointment comes as Nvidia shares were already recovering from their recent decline. Nvidia stock was up some 8% in premarket trading.

The news comes as crypto markets start to bounce back after several days of intense selling pressure.

As per the supplied market snapshot, Bitcoin is trading at $62,795.99, up 1.5% in the last hour.

Still, the biggest cryptocurrency is up just 0.3% in the last 24 hours and down 5% over the past week.

Recent findings suggest that on the brighter side, XRP is up 2% in the last hour at $0.9691. The Ripple-associated coin is 1.2% higher over the past 24 hours, though it is still down 1.8% over the past week.

Industry observers note that shiba Inu is also trading at $0.00000362. The coin has recorded a small daily increase of around 0.8%, as per CoinGlass data.

Other major crypto assets are also bouncing back. Ethereum is up 1.8% in the last hour at $1,767. Solana, meanwhile, is up 2.2% at $74.69.

The move higher comes after Bitcoin dropped to around $55,500 this past weekend, falling to its lowest price in over two years.

Volkswagen may have just hinted at the name of its next affordable EV

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that volkswagen is getting ready to launch a upcoming electric car starting at about €20,000 ($22,000) in 2027, and it looks like the entry-level EV may no longer be nameless.
  • The fresh entry-level EV is “the last piece of the puzzle,” Volkswagen brand CEO Thomas Schäfer mentioned last March after unveiling the ID.
  • Volkswagen mentioned the production version will launch in 2027 with a starting price of around €20,000 ($22,000).
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that volkswagen is getting ready to launch a upcoming electric car starting at about €20,000 ($22,000) in 2027, and it looks like the entry-level EV may no longer be nameless. A newly filed trademark could have just given away what VW plans to call it.

The fresh entry-level EV is “the last piece of the puzzle,” Volkswagen brand CEO Thomas Schäfer mentioned last March after unveiling the ID. EVERY1 concept car.

Volkswagen mentioned the production version will launch in 2027 with a starting price of around €20,000 ($22,000).

The newly introduced model will sit below the ID. Polo in Volkswagen’s Electric Urban Car Family, a lineup of compact, affordable electric cars.

It has been revealed that volkswagen’s current entry-level EV lineup includes the ID. Polo, ID. Cross, the Cupra Raval, and Skoda Epiq, all based on its new MEB+ platform.

Sources indicate that after launching the lower-priced standard versions of the ID. Polo and ID. Cross recently, starting at €24,995 and €27,995, respectively, Volkswagen is preparing to launch an even smaller, more affordable EV next year.

A recent trademark filing with the European Union Intellectual Property Office (EUIPO) and the German DPMA may have just revealed the name of VW’s upcoming €20,000 EV.

Industry observers note that volkswagen filed a trademark application for the name ID. UP on October 22, 2026, with the EUIPO and DPMA, suggesting this will be the name of the upcoming electric car in 2027.

The trademark follows previous reports that VW planned to revive the former Up! name as part of its shift away from its previous numerical naming scheme (ID.3, ID.4, ID.5, etc.).

Volkswagen has kept most details a secret thus far. Like the ID. Polo, the first to go on sale with an established VW nameplate, the ID. UP is expected to use the same 37 kWh LFP battery to reduce costs.

Sources indicate that the VW ID. Polo with the 37 kWh battery offers a WLTP range of up to 334 km (207 miles), so the smaller ID. UP will likely provide around the same, if not slightly more.

Volkswagen remarked it will offer at least 250 km (155 miles) of range. It will also use a newly introduced 70 kW (94 hp) electric motor, enabling a top speed of 130 km/h (80 mph).

The production version of the ID. EVERY1, expected to arrive as the ID. UP, will be one of nine upcoming models VW intends to launch by 2027.

Volkswagen previously noted the entry-level EV will be 3,880 mm long, which would position it between the former Up! (3,600 mm) and the ID. Polo (4,053 mm). Despite its compact size, VW said the electric city car will seat four passengers and offer a luggage compartment volume of 305 liters.

The VW Group’s fresh Electric Urban Car Family is off to a strong start, securing nearly 150,000 orders after series production began in June.

All models within the family are built on the MEB+ platform with a FWD powertrain, and share more than 80% of the components and tech.

Recent findings suggest that volkswagen said the production version of the ID. EVERY1 will be among the first vehicles based on its zonal, software-defined vehicle (SDV) architecture, which it is developing through its joint venture with Rivian.

Ah, finally a car in the upper range of being meaningful and sensible.

If someone needs more, then those are obviously special needs people. Being like can't enter and exit such a sensible car. Or like having to move the 15 horses of their 5 daughters. Or being a fieldworker driving a gazillion miles every day. Or requiring a lot of attention from lesser beings.

In March, the Rivian and Volkswagen Group Technologies (RV Tech) joint venture tested the latest SDV architecture on the ID. EVERY1, alongside Audi and Scout reference vehicles, validating over-the-air (OTA) capabilities.

The upcoming architecture will enable “highly automated driving features” and “advanced infotainment solutions,” with continuous OTA updates.

While VW said it will deploy the SDV architecture in “electric vehicles across markets in the Western Hemisphere,” the entry-level EV is not expected to reach the States.

Volkswagen is, however, preparing to launch the ID. Tiguan, which will launch in 2027 as the successor to the ID.4 (and ID.5 in Europe).

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Electrek ↗ Open Full Page

Rinnai’s new heat pump water heaters get smarter – and easier to install

📅 14 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (781 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Electrek

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Rinnai has launched a new lineup of electric heat pump water heaters that adds wifi controls and more installation options to an appliance that can cut the energy needed for hot showers.
  • The REHPW series comes in 50-, 65-, and 80-gallon sizes.
  • In a recent development, heat pump water heaters pull heat from the surrounding air and transfer it into the tank.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Rinnai has launched a new lineup of electric heat pump water heaters that adds wifi controls and more installation options to an appliance that can cut the energy needed for hot showers.

The REHPW series comes in 50-, 65-, and 80-gallon sizes. It builds on Rinnai’s existing REHP lineup, with changes designed to make the units easier to install, monitor, and maintain.

In a recent development, heat pump water heaters pull heat from the surrounding air and transfer it into the tank. Moving that heat requires less electricity than producing it with conventional electric resistance elements. There’s no fuel combustion at the appliance, although emissions from its electricity supply depend on the grid.

According to recent reports, rinnai lists a Uniform Energy Factor, or UEF, of 3.75 for the 50-gallon model and 4.0 for the two larger versions. Higher numbers mean greater efficiency under standardized testing; actual bills depend on electricity rates, hot water use, and installation conditions.

Industry observers note that the lineup delivers up to 91 gallons of hot water in the first hour, depending on tank size. That rating includes both stored hot water and what the unit can heat during that hour – useful context when several people take consecutive showers.

It has been revealed that there are five operating modes, 4.5 kW backup heating elements, and a variable-speed fan designed to keep noise down. The heat pump can operate with ambient air as low as 37°F.

Installation is where some of the more practical upgrades show up.

Industry observers note that the latest Rinnai heat pump water heater units have water connections on both the top and side, giving installers more options for connecting existing plumbing. Both the air intake and exhaust are on top, allowing zero side clearance where Rinnai’s installation requirements permit.

Sources indicate that an optional ducting kit adds flexibility for tighter spaces. Carrying handles help with moving the tank into place, and the air filter slides out horizontally from the side for cleaning.

Rinnai has also added a third tank temperature sensor to the 50- and 80-gallon models to help manage hot water delivery.

Wifi adds remote monitoring and control. Rinnai’s updated Central app supports the REHPW series, including scheduling and tools to use time-of-use electricity rates to manage energy use.

Recent findings suggest that the units also carry CTA-2045 AC Level 2 certification for demand response. That gives compatible utility programs a way to communicate with the water heater and adjust its electricity use. Rinnai indicates the certification can help qualify homeowners for local and state utility demand-response rebates; availability depends on the program.

The series is Energy Star certified, meets NEEA Tier 4 requirements, and complies with California’s Title 24 requirements, including JA13, according to Rinnai. Warranty coverage includes 10 years for the tank and other parts, plus one year for labor.

It has been revealed that I’m very happy with my hybrid heat pump water heater. I run it in heat pump only mode in summer and it helps cool the house for free. For anyone on the fence, especially your utility offers a rebate, it’s definitely worth looking at.

It has been revealed that rinnai directs buyers to an installer for pricing, so the upfront cost – and how much a local rebate might offset it – will require a quote. However, the REHP series price on Amazon hovers around the $2,000 mark.

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (393 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Ambcrypto

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sui [SUI] crypto token is making headlines for various reasons, with the most important being Hashi’s launch on the Sui mainnet, an attempt to make Bitcoin [BTC] more useful in decentralized finance (DeFi).
  • Earlier, Bitcoin holders had limited options when it comes to earning returns or accessing liquidity without selling their BTC.
  • Sources indicate that the process works through a token called hBTC.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sui [SUI] crypto token is making headlines for various reasons, with the most important being Hashi’s launch on the Sui mainnet, an attempt to make Bitcoin [BTC] more useful in decentralized finance (DeFi).

Earlier, Bitcoin holders had limited options when it comes to earning returns or accessing liquidity without selling their BTC. However, now with Hashi, there’s an option that allows users to use their Bitcoin as collateral for loans and other financial products while retaining their exposure to BTC.

Sources indicate that the process works through a token called hBTC. When a user deposits Bitcoin into Hashi, the protocol mints an equivalent amount of hBTC on the Sui blockchain at a 1:1 ratio.

Industry observers note that to make the process even more seamless, Hashi uses Sui validators and a 2-of-2 multisignature setup to prevent any single entity from moving deposited Bitcoin independently. It also requires six Bitcoin network confirmations before issuing hBTC.

Its first major use case is lending through Fluid, where people can deposit hBTC as collateral and borrow USDC without selling their BTC. However, falling Bitcoin prices could trigger collateral liquidations.

Remarking on the same, Michaël van de Poppe, CIO & Founder at MN Fund, stated,.

It’s one of the reasons why $SUI is my largest position in my Altcoin portfolio.

It has been revealed that besides this, the Sui crypto token has also made waves in the ETF ecosystem, wherein Grayscale’s Sui Staking ETF attracted $5.33 million in inflows during the week ending 20th November. Even as U.S. spot crypto ETFs collectively recorded $1.51 billion in net outflows.

In fact, its 19th November inflow of more than $5.43 million was reportedly its strongest single-day performance since its February launch.

That noted, Sui is also showing growth in its stablecoin ecosystem as its stablecoin supply increased by 7.36% to approximately $584.26 million.

In fact, according to a previous report by AMBCrypto, Sui’s stablecoin market cap outperformed the broader crypto stablecoin market, which contracted by around 5%.

All these coincided with SUI trading at $0.6589 at press time, after a hike of 3.4% in the past 24 hours. Yet, despite the price hike, Open Interest has steadily declined to approximately $350-$400 million by late November.

This indicates that traders are closing their positions in SUI derivatives, pointing to a decline in speculative activity and leveraged exposure.

Shiba Inu (SHIB) gained 5.96% over the past 24 hours and traded at $0.0000038 on Monday, according to CoinMarketCap, as talk of a December "Santa rally" returned to the crypto market. Still, SHIB is down 8.86% over the past seven days, and the token has lost 18.5% in November so far, according to CryptoRank.

Last week, SHIB dropped to $0.00000337, its lowest level since 2021.

The hopes for a Santa rally come after Goldman Sachs analysts mentioned last week that most of the December gains on the stock market usually come after Dec. 15. SHIB's own December history, however, reveals that the Santa rally came for the token once in five years.

In a recent development, according to CryptoRank, SHIB lost 29.5% and 13.5% in December of 2021 and 2022, respectively. In December of 2023, the token gained 24.6%. In December of 2024 and 2025, SHIB lost 21% and 17.6%, respectively.

SHIB's median December return is -17.6%, and its average December return is -11.4%, according to CryptoRank data.

Recent findings suggest that the green December of 2023 came after SHIB gained 6.04% in October and 6.62% in November of that year, according to CryptoRank. In 2026, SHIB lost 18.6% in October, and November is also in the red so far.

The Goldman note, titled "GS Flow of Funds: Chopsgiving," came from Gail Hafif, Brian Garrett and Lee Coppersmith, who looked at S&P 500 data going back to 1928. According to the note, the index usually gains 1.1% from mid-November to early December and then gives back about two-thirds of that gain by mid-December, and around 80% of the full 2.4% gain comes after Dec. 14-15.

Since 1990, the S&P 500 has risen after Dec. 15 in 27 of 36 years, according to Goldman.

The Goldman team called these figures a historical map. In the years when the VIX volatility index was above 18 in the middle of November, the S&P 500 gained 1.34% on average, and the index ended the year higher in 59% of cases, according to the note. According to Goldman, the VIX was above that level in mid-November of this year as well.

Goldman also mentioned that retail investors have been buying significant tech and chip stocks. Large funds and systematic traders have been cutting their positions, according to the note.

The Stock Trader's Almanac counts the last five trading days of December and the first two trading days of January as the Santa Claus rally. This season, the window will open on Dec. 24 and close on Jan. 5.

In the window that ended on Jan. 5, 2026, the S&P 500 declined 0.11%, according to the Almanac. "Santa was a no-show for the third year in a row," the Almanac wrote. Before that, the S&P 500 also ended the Santa Claus rally windows of 2023 and 2024 lower.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • And it only works inside Tesla’s Robotaxi service areas in Texas and Florida, the same geofences that have turned out to be significantly smaller than what Tesla advertises.
  • Tesla’s official Robotaxi account announced the invites on X on Friday with screenshots of the order page and the invitation email.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Tesla is now inviting “select customers” to buy a Cybercab for personal use at $29,990, but the car won’t move unless you also pay $299 a month for an “Autonomy Subscription.”.

And it only works inside Tesla’s Robotaxi service areas in Texas and Florida, the same geofences that have turned out to be significantly smaller than what Tesla advertises.

Tesla’s official Robotaxi account announced the invites on X on Friday with screenshots of the order page and the invitation email.

The order page lists the Cybercab at $29,990 before taxes, with an estimated delivery of December 2026 in Austin, Texas. You need to put down a $1,000 non-refundable deposit to order.

Industry observers note that the subscription isn’t optional. It’s pre-checked on the order page at $299 per month, with one month included, and the fine print notes “Subscription and regular vehicle maintenance required to operate.”.

It has been revealed that the email is even more direct. Its asterisk reads: “Only available in supported service areas. Subscription required for operation.”.

According to recent reports, the rest is what we already knew. Two seats, a 21-inch center touchscreen, 20.1 cubic feet of cargo space, and no steering wheel or pedals. Tesla calls it “fully autonomous” and says you’ll “manage your ride in the app.”.

Musk had promised a Cybercab “below $30,000” when he unveiled it in 2024. He technically hit it. He just didn’t mention the $3,588 a year it takes to use it. Over five years, that’s about $47,600 for a two-seater, before insurance, maintenance, taxes, and charging.

Tesla runs its Robotaxi service in eight cities: Austin, Dallas, Houston, Fort Worth, and San Antonio in Texas, and Miami, Orlando, and Tampa in Florida. That’s where a Cybercab can operate. Everywhere else, it’s a $30,000 sculpture in your driveway.

In a recent development, and those service areas aren’t what Tesla says they are. Independent tracker Koby Pierce tested thousands of addresses in the Robotaxi app and found that the areas where Tesla actually accepts pickups and drop-offs are only 59% to 78% of the advertised geofences in the six cities he checked. In Austin, the very city where Tesla is delivering these cars, it’s about 59%.

According to recent reports, railroad crossings are a significant reason why. In Houston, the creator of Robotaxi Tracker found the app quoting about 40 minutes to go two blocks downtown because the vehicle appeared to route around rail crossings. Tesla also lists San Antonio’s airport inside its polygon but doesn’t serve it.

Then there’s the regulatory cloud. NHTSA has ordered Tesla to prove under oath that a car with no brake pedal meets federal safety standards that require one. Tesla answered on October 30 and asked that the entire response be kept confidential. NHTSA hasn’t ruled. Tesla is now selling the car to consumers anyway.

I think this is going to be a total mess. It looks like Tesla is only doing this by invitation and delivering it in Austin to prove they can deliver an “unsupervised” vehicle in 2026.

Tesla is going to sell these to fans who are excited about owning a self-driving car, and many of them will find out the limitations aren’t worth $299 a month on top of a $30,000 car.

In a recent development, sure, if your monthly Uber bill is well over $300 and you live and work deep inside the geofence, maybe the math works on paper. Until you realize you have to park it somewhere once you get to your destination. Or that it can’t take you to a friend’s place two neighborhoods over. Or that a 15-minute drive turns into an hour because the car won’t cross a train track. With an Uber or a Waymo, that’s someone else’s problem. With a Cybercab, you’re paying for the privilege.

It has been revealed that no point trying to calculate what it will cost over X years. Tesla can change that monthly fee at will anyway (and shall be expected to, considering their overall pricing history).

Recent findings suggest that and here’s the part that makes no sense to me. The Cybercab runs on the same AI4 computer as the current Model Y. Tesla already runs unsupervised Model Y Robotaxis in these same geofences. So why can’t the Model Y owners who already paid for “Full Self-Driving” get unsupervised operation in those same zones? Wouldn’t be even easier to turn that on these vehicles which have accumulated much more data? Tesla keeps pushing that to “next year,” at the moment around Q2 2027, while asking people to buy a newly introduced two-seater that can do nothing else.

According to recent reports, if the tech works unsupervised in Austin, turn it on for the Model Y owners in Austin. If it doesn’t, why should anyone pay $47,000 over five years for a car that only works where Tesla indicates it does?

Like with every other Tesla product lately, the delivered version is going to be a lot more disappointing than the one that was sold on stage.

Recent findings suggest that if you’re buying an EV, powering it with home solar can cut your fuel costs to nearly zero, and it works anywhere, no geofence required. With electricity rates up almost 10% last year and expected to keep climbing, going solar is one of the best ways to protect yourself against rising costs. 📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Home » Cryptopedia » 5 Best VPNs Worth Using for Crypto.

As global tracking and exchange geofencing tighten, choosing the right VPN matters more than ever.

If you’re involved in crypto, you know how quickly things can go wrong: one wrong click, an unsecured public Wi-Fi connection or a data leak can expose your wallet, trading activity or identity.

In 2026 the stakes are higher. Crypto adoption is growing, DeFi is expanding, AI capabilities are advancing, and more jurisdictions are looking to monitor financial activity.

A reliable VPN is no longer just an optional privacy tool. It is a basic part of operational security. Here’s a straightforward look at five VPNs worth considering for crypto owners.

Your internet service provider (ISP), exchange or local network may be able to see your IP address and traffic patterns. Public Wi-Fi remains a common security risk, while geo-restrictions on exchanges are still widespread. If your IP address is linked to a wallet or trading account, the risk of further identification increases.

A good VPN encrypts your connection, hides your real IP address and reduces this exposure. It does not replace hardware wallets, two-factor authentication (2FA) or sound operational security. It is just one layer of protection.

To identify the strongest options for 2026, we evaluated providers against these key criteria:.

Industry observers note that instead, Mullvad generates a random 16-digit account number. You can add funds using Bitcoin (BTC), Bitcoin Cash (BCH), Monero (XMR) or even physical cash sent by mail. The price is a flat €5 per month, with no long-term discounts or renewal price increases. Cryptocurrency payments qualify for a 10% discount.

Mullvad runs its own full node for each supported cryptocurrency and hosts all its wallets, so no third party is involved.

The organization is based in Sweden. It argues that Swedish law allows it to operate a privacy-focused service because the electronic communications law requiring data collection does not apply to it.

Mullvad has undergone multiple independent security audits. In a 2023 police raid, authorities reportedly found no customer data to seize. The service uses RAM-only servers, open-source apps and the WireGuard protocol. It supports up to five devices.

Best for: Users who want to provide as little personal information as possible when signing up.

According to recent reports, proton VPN has one of the most consistent public audit records among the providers reviewed. The Swiss-based manufacturer passed its fifth consecutive annual no-logs audit by Securitum in June 2026.

In a recent development, payment options are more limited. Bitcoin is available only after you create a free account and upgrade to a paid blueprint. Proton also accepts cash in CHF, USD and EUR.

According to recent reports, proton VPN operates more than 20,000 servers in over 130 countries. Its apps are open source, and paid aims support up to 10 devices.

Unlike providers that use RAM-only servers, Proton VPN relies on full-disk encryption. For leak protection, it offers a standard kill switch and a permanent kill switch on Windows and Linux, which blocks internet access if the VPN connection drops.

Best for: Consumers who value audited transparency and Swiss jurisdiction and are comfortable providing an email address.

NordVPN stands out for its performance and range of security features. Based in Panama, where no data-retention laws apply, it uses RAM-only servers. Its no-logs policy has been independently verified six times, most recently by Deloitte Lithuania in late 2025.

According to recent reports, features include an internet kill switch, obfuscated servers, Dedicated IP options and Threat Protection, which blocks malicious websites and phishing links. NordVPN supports up to 10 simultaneous connections.

Payment options include Bitcoin, Ethereum, Litecoin and stablecoins.

Best for: Active traders who prioritise speed, Dedicated IP options and a broad set of features.

In a recent development, surfshark combines competitive pricing with a growing record of independent audits. Its Trust Center lists Deloitte audits from 2023 and 2025 that verified its no-logs policy. KPMG audit also confirmed Surfshark does not store browsing history, IP addresses, connection timestamps or outgoing traffic.

Crypto customers can pay with Bitcoin, Ethereum, Cardano, Dogecoin, XRP and Shiba Inu through supported third-party wallets. However, an email address is required to register.

Industry observers note that surfshark is based in the Netherlands. The firm claims local law does not require it to log or retain user activity. Its entire server network uses RAM-only infrastructure.

Security features include an automatic kill switch and Everlink, which switches owners to another server during maintenance without interrupting their session.

Best for: Budget-conscious crypto people who want audited privacy protections, flexible cryptocurrency payments and unlimited device connections.

IVPN is a smaller, privacy-focused provider based in Gibraltar. Its approach is similar to Mullvad’s.

Signup generates a random account ID and requires no email address or other personal information. Payment options include Monero, Bitcoin, physical cash, credit cards and PayPal. The company also runs its own nodes for cryptocurrency payments.

IVPN’s apps are fully open source. Built-in features include AntiTracker, a kill switch/firewall and V2Ray obfuscation.

The firm has commissioned annual security audits by Cure53. These reviews assess its apps and infrastructure; they are not equivalent to a Big Four audit specifically designed to verify no-logs claims.

Recent findings suggest that in August 2026, a vulnerability in BTCPay Server allowed an attacker to drain 0.6168 BTC from IVPN’s Lightning node. IVPN states no customer data was accessed.

Best for: Privacy-first users who want anonymous account-number signup and crypto payments.

Sources indicate that A VPN hides your IP address, protects traffic on public Wi-Fi and limits what your internet provider can see. But it does not make your crypto wallet anonymous.

Use a VPN to protect your network privacy. Protect your on-chain privacy through careful wallet management and by checking every transaction before signing.

It can if you use a shared IP address that jumps across countries or lands on an exchange’s blacklist. Centralized exchanges (CEXs) frequently flag sudden IP changes as suspicious login attempts or sanctions-evasion risks. If you trade regularly on a CEX, stick to a single server location or use a Dedicated IP add-on so your login address stays consistent.

Almost never. Most free VPNs monetize users by logging traffic, injecting ads, or selling connection metadata to third parties—which defeats the purpose of crypto operational security. The only exception on this list is Proton VPN’s free tier, which has no data caps, no ads, and is covered by the same independent no-logs audits as its paid intends, though it limits server locations and doesn’t support direct crypto payments without upgrading.

Yes. HTTPS encrypts the contents of your connection, but it does not hide your IP address or the domains you connect to. Without a VPN, your internet provider can still see that you are connecting to crypto exchanges or DeFi front-ends, and your wallet’s default RPC node can still log your home IP alongside your public wallet address.

.@injective led tokenized fund growth this past week. @StellarOrg had a good week also. https://t.co/7Ip2oK6c1X.

This means Stellar continues to grow in tokenized assets, a major highlight of strong growth in Q3, 2026.

Real-world assets tokenized on Stellar amounted to $4.1 billion at the end of Q3 2026, up 36% from Q2 and up 548% from Q3 2025. Two assets drove the bulk of the quarter’s growth: Tradable’s new tokenized private credit and continued inflows into the Spiko Amundi overnight swap fund.

Recent findings suggest that in late August 2026, Stellar held more tokenized non-US government debt than any other blockchain, with about $490 million in sovereign instruments. Stellar has widened access to tokenized funds in the United States, Europe and Asia. Franklin Templeton’s BENJI has been on Stellar since 2021. This expands the set of institutions permitted to hold it. Franklin Templeton made a similar move in Europe, registering 'grBenji' as a Luxembourg UCITS share class for third-party distribution, now live on 21X.

In Asia, Marketnode announced in August that it will offer funds from BNY Investments on Stellar, with Marketnode acting as the tokenization and distribution platform. Together, these developments expand access to tokenized funds on Stellar for institutions in the United States, Europe and Asia.

I finally got a USB-C charging e-bike, and it costs 75% less than Rivian’s bike

📅 14 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1062 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Electrek

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that I’ve been waiting years for electric bikes to finally embrace USB-C charging.
  • Meet the ENGWE Zip, a quirky little folding electric bike that costs just €999 and has swiftly become one of my favorite examples of how a small feature can make a big difference.
  • When it debuted earlier this year, it became only the third production e-bike I’ve seen that could charge via USB-C, allowing it to use the same charger that is likely already shared by your phone and laptop.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that I’ve been waiting years for electric bikes to finally embrace USB-C charging. We’ve already standardized much of our lives around the convenient little connector, from phones and laptops to tablets and countless other gadgets. But for some reason, electric bikes have largely missed the memo. Now, though, I’m finally riding an e-bike that charges with USB-C, and the best part is that it doesn’t cost an arm and a leg.

Meet the ENGWE Zip, a quirky little folding electric bike that costs just €999 and has swiftly become one of my favorite examples of how a small feature can make a big difference.

When it debuted earlier this year, it became only the third production e-bike I’ve seen that could charge via USB-C, allowing it to use the same charger that is likely already shared by your phone and laptop.

Industry observers note that USB-C charging on electric bikes isn’t entirely new, but it’s surprisingly rare. Ampler was one of the first companies to introduce it barely a year ago, though its bikes are sadly no longer in production after the firm’s bankruptcy. More recently, Rivian’s ALSO electric bike arrived with USB-C charging, but that bike costs around $4,500 – at least if you want the model that’s slowly starting to ship.

The ENGWE Zip, on the other hand, costs roughly a quarter as much as its only USB-charging competition. At €999, it’s priced at a relatively affordable US$1,100. That’s a quarter of the cost of the only other USB-C charging e-bike on the market.

Of course, it’s not nearly as technologically advanced as Rivian’s ALSO e-bike. But hey, it’s at least shipping.

And while the Zip is a fun little 16″ wheel folding electric bike in its own right, with a compact design that makes it easy to store and transport, it’s the charging setup that has me particularly excited.

According to recent reports, instead of keeping track of yet another proprietary charging brick, I can simply grab the USB-C charger from my laptop and plug it into the bike. There’s one in my living room by the couch. There’s one by my bed. There’s one in all of my friends’ places. There’s a USB-C charger everywhere.

If I’m traveling around, that means one less charger to pack. If I’m visiting someone, there’s a decent chance they already have a compatible charger sitting around.

Sources indicate that heck, I can even use a basic USB-C phone charger in a pinch. Sure, charging a relatively large e-bike battery at 20W isn’t going to be particularly quick, but the fact that I can do it at all is incredibly convenient.

Plus, the bike has one more trick. The battery also outputs USB-C, so I can charge my laptop or other devices from it as well. I can even charge two devices simultaneously, thanks to the dual USB-C ports.

It has been revealed that the battery is housed in a roll-top bag that is locked into the headset of the bike but can be promptly unlocked for charging off the bike. And since it’s a keyed lock, no one can steal the battery even when the bag is left on the bike.

I typically charge the battery still mounted on the bike, though occasionally when I want to use a friend’s USB-C charger, I’ll just pop the bag off and bring it right up to wherever the closest USB-C charger is located.

It may not be the fastest charge, but it’s pretty darn convenient. And with a 360Wh battery, a powerful 100W laptop charger will still get it pretty much full in 4 hours, or for a more typical 50% recharge, roughly two hours.

And that’s really the beauty of USB-C charging. It’s not necessarily about charging faster. It’s about having options. It’s about not being stuck if the very specific charger that only works on your e-bike doesn’t happen to be around exactly where you are.

Of course, there’s a technical reason we haven’t seen USB-C charging spread across the e-bike industry quite as quickly as it has with smaller electronics. Most e-bike batteries operate at 36V or 48V nominal, meaning their charging voltages are higher than the 20V typically supplied by common USB-C laptop chargers. That requires additional voltage conversion and charging circuitry inside the bike or battery.

But clearly, it can be done. And if ENGWE can offer it on a €999 electric bike, there’s a pretty compelling argument that more manufacturers should be taking a serious look at the technology. In this case, it’s all housed inside the battery, meaning it could be directly incorporated into any e-bike whose manufacturer is brave enough to spec it.

In a recent development, USB-C charging aside, there's a very good reason that just about every folding e-bike on the market has put thick plates on the folding connection of the frame. It's because the frame breaks if they're not there. Just like this one is going to.

I’m not suggesting that every e-bike needs to abandon its dedicated charger tomorrow. For larger batteries, high-powered chargers still make plenty of sense, especially when you want to get back on the road swiftly.

According to recent reports, but having USB-C as an additional charging option? That’s something I’d love to see become standard.

For years, we’ve seen how electric bikes are becoming more convenient, more practical, and better integrated into our everyday lives. Yet when it comes to charging, we’re still carrying around a collection of more or less proprietary chargers.

Now I’m riding a barely $1k electric bike that can charge from the same power brick as my laptop. And frankly, I think it’s about time the rest of the e-bike industry caught up!

Further data indicates that Bitcoin spot ETFs suffered the largest withdrawals as investors pulled out about $1.79 billion during the same period.

The negative trend also extended to the Ethereum ETF market as the funds posted a total of $314.17 million in net outflows following the consistent selling pressure.

In addition to this, the XRP spot ETFs were not spared, as the funds recorded $11.11 million in weekly outflows, leaving Solana as the only one among the four major crypto ETFs to finish the week on a positive note.

Jensen Huang’s reinstatement at Nvidia sparks a broad AI rebound, adding fresh momentum to Jefferies’ 64% upside call on SpaceX stock.

SpaceX stock (SPCX) is rallying sharply today, surging nearly 8.09% to around $138 as broader AI and tech markets rebound following Nvidia’s unanimous decision to reinstate Jensen Huang as CEO.

The momentum adds fresh fuel to a bullish call from Jefferies, which just initiated coverage on SpaceX with a Buy rating and a $210 price target—implying roughly 64% upside from pre-rally levels.

In a research note titled It’s Just Rocket Science, Jefferies identified Starlink as the core engine behind SpaceX’s long-term valuation.

Jefferies projects Starlink could generate $92 billion in annual revenue by 2029—growing at a 70% compound annual rate—with operating margins exceeding 60%, according to Investing.com.

The core launch division is forecast to deliver $9 billion in revenue and $4 billion in EBITDA by 2029 as Starship scales toward 315 flights per year.

As hyperscalers race to secure electricity, data centers, and compute capacity, SpaceX’s orbital network and massive capital deployment position it to capture growing AI infrastructure demand.

While Jefferies’ thesis originally framed SpaceX as a resilient play during the broader AI selloff, market sentiment flipped overnight. Nvidia’s board reinstated Jensen Huang just 11 days after his resignation—sending NVDA shares up roughly 30% and lifting the Nasdaq nearly 7%.

On Friday, the S&P 500 and Dow Jones Industrial Average slipped more than 10% below their record highs into correction territory, while the Nasdaq dropped roughly 5%, erasing its 2026 gains.

Nvidia sat at the epicenter of the rout, plunging roughly 13%–14% on Friday following CEO Jensen Huang’s resignation amid scrutiny over an alleged Chinese chip-smuggling link, alongside reports that SEC enforcement staff are reviewing potential accounting issues.

Newly public Anthropic also surrendered most of its first-day IPO gains during its second session, while expectations of a December Federal Reserve rate hike added pressure across high-growth tech.

According to recent reports, for crypto traders, SpaceX’s stock trajectory matters on two fronts. First, high-beta tech and AI equities continue to dictate institutional risk appetite—sharp drawdowns in Nasdaq heavyweights often trigger short-term deleveraging across Bitcoin and AI-linked tokens.

Second, Jefferies’ thesis reinforces one of crypto’s strongest narratives: compute and bandwidth scarcity, a bottleneck driving capital toward both orbital infrastructure and decentralized physical infrastructure networks (DePIN).

Sources indicate that A basket contains 40,000 shares. At Friday’s basket size of 514.73 ETH, the fund’s unstaked holdings were equivalent to nearly 113 baskets. Using the reported balance of 58,138.78 ETH, 112 whole baskets would fit at that size.

The sponsor targets an unstaked reserve of 5% to 30% of the trust’s ETH, a buffer it calls the Liquidity Sleeve. The trust can also hold unstaked ETH for pending orders, expenses or shareholder distributions. The amount available for any set of orders depends on commitments, rebalancing and any other liquidity the sponsor can arrange.

Industry observers note that farside Investors had yet to report ETHB’s Nov. 20 net flow as of Sunday. The issuer listed Friday’s closing discount to net asset value at 0.12%, a measure of how the exchange price compared with per-share net asset value.

Sources indicate that the fund’s prospectus allows the sponsor to require cash orders when its reserve runs low. Under stress it can delay delivery of ETH or move to cash-only redemptions. Cash settlement can also be delayed if available ETH is insufficient. An authorized participant offered delayed settlement can cancel the order or choose to wait. For outstanding delayed in-kind orders, the sponsor intends to start unstaking and prioritize orders by date.

ETHB can pay in cash or ether. If available ether runs short, the sponsor can change the settlement method or delay delivery.

A validator withdrawal can add time when ETHB needs to unstake for delayed redemptions.

The stress path illustrates conditional procedures. The Nov. 20 Ethereum sample is a dated estimate. Actual settlement timing depends on available funds and the sponsor’s decisions.

Its sample put the exit queue at about 2.6 days, followed by a roughly 27-hour protocol wait and up to about 6.7 days for the network to send the ETH. The trust sets settlement timing for delayed orders.

For shareholders, the more direct consequence would be a possible wait for ETHB staking payouts. The liquidity policy notes the sponsor aims to put redemptions ahead of staking distributions and fees during stress. Distributions and fees would keep accruing while settlement is delayed. The sponsor says the trust would file a Form 8-K if that stress prevented settlement on its usual cycle, giving investors a disclosure to watch alongside the next holdings figures.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that it’s possible to see a blockchain transfer within minutes, but that doesn’t mean a casino will process a withdrawal request that fast. Various factors, including fees and the game being played, impact how rapidly a withdrawal can be processed. With that in mind, readers should evaluate claims beyond the headline.

In a recent development, when reviewing a crypto casino in Canada, the first step should be to analyze the payment terms and ensure the casino is approved to take your business in your province. Just because a casino supports crypto payments doesn’t mean it’s licensed to take your business, offers instant payouts, or has games that have been vetted by an independent testing agency. Each of those should be supported by additional evidence.

Internal approval and blockchain processing are separate steps in a withdrawal request.

Look at each step of the withdrawal process in turn. Determine if a guaranteed timeframe covers the entire process or only certain requests.

Recent findings suggest that A payment transaction hash is the best way to trace a payment. Prior to the payment being transmitted, account status or support can give information about the payment processing.

There are several costs associated with a crypto payment that should be taken into consideration. A wallet or exchange may charge a fee to send funds, a blockchain may charge a fee to process the transaction, and the casino may charge a withdrawal fee.

In a recent development, conversion also needs to be considered. Deposits converted to a Canadian dollar balance need to consider exchange rates, conversion timing, and spread. Leaving funds in cryptocurrency means their Canadian dollar value can change, while the coin balance remains the same.

Look at minimum withdrawals and fees. A small payout can incur a high cost, especially with fixed fees. Promotions can also impact which funds are available for withdrawal.

Evaluate evidence supporting claims of game fairness. Consider how outcomes are determined and whether published rules are implemented. Look for game providers who are independently tested and named, rather than relying on a badge.

A stated return to player is based on the long-term average and does not prohibit large losses.

Some games offer “provably fair” verification. Note what the verification actually checks, and whether you can reproduce the check yourself. Verifying a specific outcome does not mean you can validate withdrawal reliability, the legality of the game, or the security of the components of the game.

Readers from Canada should check their local gambling authority. In Ontario, for example, iGaming Ontario has a directory of licensed operators, and OLG operates separately. Usually, the actual website is more vital than recognizing the brand.

It has been revealed that look at account currency and payment totals to determine withdrawal terms. Keep a copy of the terms to show and explain discrepancies to support your case.

It’s important to assess speed of payout, fees, and fairness of a service separately. Assessing a service by the acceptance of cryptocurrency, in general, is a poor quality standard. It’s important to set limits on time and money spent, and to set funds apart, for example, for gambling, from funds that should be for saving or for daily expenses.

And Tesla wants consumers to sign it while still refusing to give unsupervised self-driving to the Model Y owners it has been selling “Full Self-Driving” to for nearly a decade.

The “Cybercab Autonomy Subscription Agreement” (version 20261112) went up on Tesla’s configurator late Friday, hours after the company started inviting select customers to order the Cybercab for personal use at $29,990 plus a mandatory $299 per month.

The key line is short: “Your Cybercab will not operate without an active Autonomy Subscription.” There’s no steering wheel and no pedals, so that isn’t a figure of speech. Stop paying and you have a $30,000 object in your garage.

Recent findings suggest that that personal-use clause kills the whole pitch. For years, Musk told people they’d buy a Tesla, add it to the fleet, and make money while they sleep. The first Tesla sold to consumers for unsupervised operation is contractually barred from doing exactly that.

Then there’s the geofence. Tesla’s Robotaxi service areas are already smaller in practice than advertised: when we tested them, real coverage was between 59% and 78% of the advertised maps, and parts of the Houston map have been called “fake” by the person tracking it. Now Tesla reserves the right to shrink that area after you’ve paid for the car.

Mark Valorian, who went through the terms on X, summed it up as “an endless variable-rate lease with a ridiculous down payment.” That’s about right.

Over five years, the car plus 59 paid months of subscription comes to $47,631 before insurance, registration, charging, and taxes, all of which are on the owner.

This is the part that should make every Tesla owner angry.

Tesla has spent the last year telling everyone that its Model Y is just as much a robotaxi as the Cybercab. Ahead of the Robotaxi launch in Austin, Musk remarked the cars were “the Model Ys we make right now, there’s no change to it.” On Tesla’s Q3 2026 earnings call last month, AI chief Ashok Elluswamy said Cybercabs and Model Y robotaxis already run the same software, and that customer cars might join the network around Q2 2027. The Cybercab introduces on the same AI4 computer found in the current Model Y.

So the hardware is the same, the software is the same, and unsupervised Model Ys are already operating in the exact geofences where Cybercab owners will be allowed to ride.

Yet the people who paid for it get nothing. Tesla started selling “Full Self-Driving Capability” in 2016 on the promise that every car it built had the hardware for it. Owners paid up to $15,000 for the package. In February, Tesla stopped selling it outright and moved to a $99 per month subscription, which still requires you to supervise the car at all times.

Sources indicate that tesla’s answer to all those owners is a newly introduced car. One with two seats, no controls, a geofence it can move whenever it wants, and a subscription that costs three times as much as FSD.

I’ll say it plainly: this car is for suckers who want to give their money to Elon Musk.

Sources indicate that you don’t own a Cybercab in any meaningful sense. You pay $30,000 for the right to keep paying Tesla $299 a month, at a price Tesla can raise, in an area Tesla can shrink, under rules Tesla enforces, with a camera pointed at you the whole time.

There are three possible reasons Tesla isn't allowing model Y owners to use FSD in the allowed zones:.

1: the robotaxis are in fact different from the model Ys being sold.

2: Tesla doesn't have enough "remote operators" to cover all of those supposedly self-driving cars if customers join the network.

3: Tesla isn't willing to accept liability when FSD kills someone.

And the Model Y part is what gives the game away. If Tesla truly believed its unsupervised system was ready for customers, the obvious move would be to turn it on for the Model Y owners in Austin who already paid for it. It’s the same computer and the same software in the same geofence. But that would mean honoring a promise made in 2016, on cars already sold, with no new revenue attached.

Sources indicate that A upcoming vehicle wipes that slate clean. No legacy FSD buyers, no HW3 baggage, just a fresh customer locked into a $299 monthly fee from day one. What Tesla built is a subscription with a $30,000 entry fee attached to it.

So what happens the first time Tesla emails Cybercab owners a month’s notice that the price is going to $399?

Express Mock Neck Mini Sweater Dress.

Sam Edelman Sylvia Knee-High Boot.

#144458. Industry News: What Are Perpetual Futures? How Crypto's Most Popular Derivative Works

Industry News: What Are Perpetual Futures? How Crypto's Most Popular Derivative Works

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1610 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Decrypt

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, perpetual futures are the engine room of crypto trading.
  • They aren't only for crypto, either.
  • This guide explains what futures are, what makes perpetual futures different, how funding rates and liquidations work, and what to know before trading them.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, perpetual futures are the engine room of crypto trading. Centralized exchanges processed $85.3 trillion in perps trading volume in 2025 alone, according to CoinGecko's State of Crypto Perpetuals Report 2026, and the U.S. Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC) describes perps as the dominant form of crypto derivatives trading.

They aren't only for crypto, either. Exchanges now offer perps on stocks, commodities and currencies, and Decrypt has become the first news publisher to offer perps trading, powered by Solana exchange Phoenix.

This guide explains what futures are, what makes perpetual futures different, how funding rates and liquidations work, and what to know before trading them.

You can now act on the news you read: Go long or short with perpetual futures, all from your Decrypt Money Account.

To understand perpetual futures, it helps to start with ordinary futures.

A futures contract is an agreement to buy or sell an asset at a set price on a set date in the future. Futures have been used for centuries: farmers used them to lock in prices for crops before harvest, and today they are traded on everything from oil and wheat to stock indexes and Bitcoin, on regulated exchanges such as CME.

Traders use futures for two main reasons. Hedgers use them to protect against price swings; an airline might buy oil futures to lock in fuel costs, for example. Speculators use them to bet on price movements without owning the underlying asset.

Traditional futures have an expiry date. When a contract expires, it settles, either by delivering the asset or, more often, by paying out the difference in cash. Traders who want to keep their position open must "roll" it into a newly introduced contract, which can add costs and complexity.

Sources indicate that perpetual futures, often shortened to "perps" or "perpetual swaps," work like futures, but with one key difference: they never expire. Traders can hold a position for as long as they like, provided they have enough collateral to keep it open.

The idea was proposed by Yale economist Robert Shiller in a 1993 paper as a way to create markets for assets that are hard to trade directly. Perps took off in crypto. Crypto exchange BitMEX, widely credited with bringing perps to crypto, launched a perpetual contract on Bitcoin in 2016. BitMEX itself closed in September 2026, but the product it pioneered has become the most traded instrument in crypto.

A perpetual contract never actually involves owning the asset. Traders deposit collateral, or "margin," and their profit or loss depends entirely on how the price moves.

When opening a perp position, a trader chooses a direction. Going long means betting the price will rise; going short means betting it will fall. Being able to short as easily as going long is one reason perps are popular: it lets traders profit from falling prices, or hedge assets they already own.

Sources indicate that perps are usually traded with leverage, which lets traders control a larger position than their collateral alone would allow. With 10x leverage, for example, $100 of margin controls a $1,000 position. If the asset's price rises 5%, the trader makes $50, a 50% return on their margin. But if it falls 5%, they lose $50, half of their margin.

Industry observers note that exchanges track two prices to manage this. The index price is the asset's price on spot markets, usually averaged across several exchanges. The mark price, based on the index and the perp market itself, is used to calculate profits and losses and to decide when positions must be closed. Using an averaged price makes it harder for a sudden spike on one exchange to trigger liquidations.

Because perps never expire, nothing forces their price to converge with the underlying asset, as traditional futures do at expiry. Instead, perps use a funding rate.

At regular intervals—most commonly every eight hours, though some platforms use shorter or longer schedules—traders on one side of the market pay traders on the other:.

Decentralized exchange Hyperliquid, for example, pays funding every hour, at one-eighth of the rate calculated for an eight-hour period, to stay consistent with centralized exchanges.

Funding payments go directly between traders, not to the exchange. For traders holding positions over long periods, these payments can add up, and they can either boost or erode returns.

Sources indicate that funding rates also offer a window into market sentiment. Strongly positive funding suggests traders are crowded into bullish bets, while negative funding indicates that bears are paying to stay short.

Rates for the same asset can also differ between exchanges. On November 19, 2026, Bitcoin's funding rate was 0.01% per eight hours on Hyperliquid, compared with 0.0037% on Binance, according to Hyperliquid's funding comparison tool.

Some traders aim to earn funding payments rather than bet on prices. In a "cash and carry" or basis trade, they buy an asset on the spot market and short the same amount through perps, collecting funding while their positions offset each other's price moves.

Recent findings suggest that leverage is a double-edged sword. Every perp position has a maintenance margin, the minimum collateral needed to keep it open. If losses push a trader's margin below that level, the exchange automatically closes the position, a process called liquidation. The trader typically loses most or all of the margin they put up.

The higher the leverage, the smaller the price move needed to trigger a liquidation. At 50x leverage, a 2% move against a position can wipe it out.

Sources indicate that liquidations can also feed on each other. When prices fall sharply, liquidated longs are forced to sell, pushing prices lower and triggering further liquidations, a so-called liquidation cascade. On October 10, 2025, the crypto market saw its largest liquidation event on record, with more than $19 billion in leveraged positions wiped out in a single day.

It has been revealed that to cover losses when positions can't be closed in time, exchanges typically keep an insurance fund. In extreme cases, some use auto-deleveraging, closing profitable positions on the other side of the market to keep the system solvent.

Crypto perps trade on two main types of venue.

Sources indicate that centralized exchanges, such as Binance, Bybit and OKX, run their own order books and hold owners' funds. They account for the vast majority of perps trading: Binance alone held about a third of centralized perps volume in early 2026, according to CoinGecko. Many are unavailable to U.S. customers.

Decentralized exchanges let traders use perps through smart contracts, while keeping control of their funds. Some, such as Hyperliquid and Solana-based Phoenix, run order books onchain, matching buyers and sellers much like a traditional exchange. Others, such as GMX and Jupiter, let traders trade against a shared pool of liquidity provided by other users.

Decentralized perps are growing fast. Their trading volume jumped from $1.5 trillion in 2024 to $6.38 trillion in 2025, led by Hyperliquid, CoinGecko found. Decentralized exchanges' share of perps trading volume peaked at 13% in late 2025 before slipping to 10% in April 2026, while their share of open interest, the total value of open positions, reached 13.5%.

Recent findings suggest that in the U.S., perps developed largely on offshore exchanges, outside the reach of the CFTC, but that has started to change. In July 2025, Coinbase introduced CFTC-regulated "perpetual-style" futures for U.S. customers, with five-year expiries and up to 10x leverage. Two months later, CFTC-regulated exchange Bitnomial launched what it called the first U.S. perpetual futures, with 25-year terms and eight-hour funding. In May 2026, the CFTC approved a Bitcoin perpetual futures contract from prediction market Kalshi and set out a framework for listing more, and in June, Kraken rolled out perps to eligible U.S. customers through Bitnomial, which its parent tech giant had acquired.

According to recent reports, some of these contracts, including Kalshi's and Bitnomial's original design, have long but fixed terms of 25 years, so are not strictly perpetual. The regulator notes perps can be offered on CFTC-registered exchanges under federal oversight, and has advised U.S. traders to avoid offshore venues.

The shift has been contested. CME Group, the largest U.S. futures exchange, has sued the CFTC, arguing that perps are swaps rather than futures under U.S. law. The CFTC has nonetheless continued to approve more perps platforms, starting with Backpack.

Perps are now spreading beyond crypto. Exchanges have begun listing perps tracking stocks, stock indexes, commodities such as gold and oil, and currencies, giving traders around-the-clock exposure to markets that normally close in the evening and on weekends.

Those products carry the same mechanics, and the same risks, as crypto perps. They track an asset's price without giving traders ownership of the asset itself, so a perp on a organization's stock doesn't come with voting rights or dividends.

Perps can be useful tools for hedging and speculation, but they are among the riskiest products in crypto:.

In a recent development, decrypt people can now trade perps directly alongside the news, through the Decrypt Money Account. The service is powered by Phoenix, a decentralized exchange on Solana, and lets users go long or short on crypto, stocks and commodities.

Availability varies by region, and as with any leveraged product, traders should only risk money they can afford to lose.

Decrypt offers perpetual futures trading through the Decrypt Money Account, powered by Phoenix.

Industry observers note that perpetual futures are leveraged products and carry a high risk of loss. Availability may vary by region. Nothing in this guide is investment advice.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • A reconstruction of 2,545 Bitcoin blocks mined by P2Pool, an early decentralized mining pool, found that none of the 15,865 payouts recorded in July 2014 fell below 0.001 BTC.
  • In a recent development, the findings, published by a former P2Pool node operator and highlighted by Bitcoin Optech on Nov.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Bitcoin's push to decentralize mining is confronting a decade-old problem that makes it harder for smaller operators to receive rewards.

A reconstruction of 2,545 Bitcoin blocks mined by P2Pool, an early decentralized mining pool, found that none of the 15,865 payouts recorded in July 2014 fell below 0.001 BTC.

In a recent development, the findings, published by a former P2Pool node operator and highlighted by Bitcoin Optech on Nov. 20, expose a constraint that developers are still struggling to overcome.

Unlike traditional mining pools, which typically distribute earnings through their own payment systems, P2Pool paid miners directly from Bitcoin's block reward transaction, known as the coinbase.

Recent findings suggest that however, each recipient requires a separate transaction output, increasing the transaction's size. Mining firmware restrictions and competition for block space limit how many miners can receive direct payments.

To manage that constraint, the original P2Pool increased the difficulty of qualifying mining shares when a miner's expected payout fell below 0.001 BTC.

As a result, smaller miners earned qualifying shares less often, making their payouts less predictable.

P2Poolv2 is developing a different approach that would allow smaller operators to sell their mining shares rather than depend on direct block rewards.

Under the proposed system, larger miners would continue receiving Bitcoin through coinbase transactions, while smaller participants could sell their shares to buyers willing to aggregate them.

Those buyers would collect the eventual Bitcoin rewards if their combined shares qualified for direct payouts.

The arrangement would give smaller miners access to earlier payments while transferring the uncertainty of future block rewards to buyers, who would seek discounted prices for assuming that risk.

According to recent reports, P2Poolv2 reports direct payouts on testnet5. Its proposed market would let smaller miners sell matured shares to buyers who can combine them.

A share sale would give the miner an earlier payment and leave the buyer waiting for future block rewards.

Testnet5 status is project-reported. A buyer needs a qualifying position and a block found while the purchased shares still count.

Recent findings suggest that schematic based on P2Poolv2’s project status, transaction architecture and market design. The two paths use the same sharechain accounting.

Testnet5 status is project-reported. A buyer needs a qualifying position and a block found while the purchased shares still count.

However, the model introduces another challenge: smaller miners would depend on buyers offering acceptable prices before their shares expire.

Developers have also warned that large miners could divide their computing power across multiple identities to secure limited direct payout slots, potentially crowding out smaller participants.

P2Poolv2 currently operates its sharechain, accounting and direct payout systems on Bitcoin's testnet5, while its proposed marketplace remains under development.

Its success will depend on whether that marketplace can attract enough buyers to pay smaller miners without concentrating reward distribution among larger operators.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Home » Ripple (XRP) » Big XRP Holders Add $72 Million While Supply Hardens.

Big-time holders draw attention to XRP’s liquidity pockets sub-$1: is a bounce back signal getting delivered?

Large XRP holders have added roughly $72 million worth of tokens in recent days, even as major Bitcoin and Ethereum investors have reduced exposure during the broader market pullback.

The buying has coincided with a drop in available XRP on Binance, where reserves have reportedly fallen below levels last seen in July.

The move does not yet signal a clear bullish reversal. XRP was trading near $0.97, down about 3.6% over the previous week and still below its 200-day moving average near $1.26.

The combination of whale accumulation and thinner exchange balances has drawn attention to whether modest returning demand could produce a sharper price response.

An exchange supply-shortage measure for XRP rose to 2.4 on November 19, 2026 above its July reading of 2.09. Usually, readings above 2 are generally associated with unusually limited immediately available supply on the venue.

#XRP supply on Binance is getting tight. The Supply Shortage Index spiked above 8 in November and sits at 2.4 now, while price is still near $0.96.Supply is tightening and price has not responded yet. pic.twitter.com/xMTksTkKim.

Large wallets also pulled more than $127 million in XRP from Binance on a net basis between November 10 and 16, 2026.

Some of those movements may reflect internal exchange reserve management rather than pure investor withdrawals, particularly after operational disruption at the platform, so the flows are not a definitive accumulation signal on their own.

Industry observers note that lower balances can still matter if spot demand returns. Fewer tokens sitting on exchanges may reduce readily available selling pressure, especially if a portion of the withdrawn XRP is moving into longer-term storage rather than being repositioned for immediate trading elsewhere.

US spot XRP ETFs have gone 15 consecutive trading days without a net inflow, their longest dry spell since launch. Since their last positive day on October 29, the funds have recorded net withdrawals of about $26.3 million.

Sources indicate that total XRP ETF assets have fallen to roughly $1.08 billion from $1.77 billion in late September, though cumulative inflows since launch remain close to $1.78 billion. Existing holders have not abandoned the products in large numbers, but fresh capital has paused.

The divergence is the central feature of the current setup: large holders have been willing to buy into weakness, while ETF demand has stayed on the sidelines.

Tighter exchange supply could amplify a recovery if broader buying returns, but without renewed fund inflows and a reclaim of key technical levels, scarcity alone is unlikely to reverse the trend.
